The article says the table represents a computation history of M on w on an accepting branch. The Lean conditions do not ensure this, and are satisfied for every NTM and every w with |w| ≥ 2. Take k = 1, let every row equal encodeConfigRow (initConfig w), and change only the last row's column 0 to qAccept. For |w| = 2 there are no interior windows at all. For |w| ≥ 3, windows centred at column 1 have a = inl q₀ in the top row, so the no-head clause is vacuous, and b is a tape symbol, so the head clause is vacuous. Windows at columns ≥ 2 have no state in the top row and e = b holds. So Tableau M w is nonempty even when M accepts nothing.

Sipser's tableau rows are successive configurations of a single accepting branch, and that correspondence is what the Cook–Levin proof needs. In the Lean: encodeConfigRow overwrites the symbol under the head with the state, so the symbol being read is lost. IsLegalWindow's head clause quantifies over every γ instead of the symbol actually under the head. Border columns are only weakly constrained, and there are no # delimiters. As a result the structure does not capture computation histories, and CookLevin.accepts_from_tableau (sorry) is false. v1's review (faithfulness 5) missed this.
